newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portuguese politicians fight euro corner.
newsitem.headline: Portuguese politicians fight euro corner.

text.p: Portugal's two main political parties are so enamoured of the euro that one opponent accused them of uniting to form "The Party of the Single Currency."

The ruling Socialists and the opposition Social Democrats both strongly back the single currency, believing it will take Portugal into the political "hard core" of Europe and foster lower interest rates and faster long-term economic growth.

They say the euro will help bring billions of dollars of direct investment to Portugal as foreign companies take advantage of its cheap labour and modern infrastructure financed by European Union (EU) cohesion funds over the past decade.
Prime Minister Antonio Guterres says he wants Portugal to join the euro from the start, on January 1, 1999.
He insists that Portugal must be considered for membership on its own merits, and not lumped together with two other so-called "Club Med" countries Spain and Italy.

Fiscal discipline and a privatisation programme that is bigger in relative terms than in most other European countries will set Portugal on course to join the euro, Guterres maintains. Most analysts agree.
"The Portuguese have been indoctrinated into the belief that the single currency is the only way forward for the country," says UBS economist Sally Wilkinson. LITTLE INTERNAL DISSENT ON EMU
The main detractors are the "Eurosceptical" rightwing Popular Party (PP) and the Communists.
The PP, which has just 15 seats in the 230-seat parliament, want a referendum on euro membership.
But even opponents of the euro concede that the Portuguese would probably vote in favour of the European single currency.
"I think 80 or 90 percent of the Portuguese would say yes to a single currency in a referendum," said Vasco d'Orey, a university economist and card-carrying member of the PP.

Jorge Ferreira, head of the PP's parliamentary group, says he believes Portugal is not ready to join the euro and fears that the country would struggle to compete with its European partners within a single currency.

During parliament's budget debate in November, he accused the government and opposition Social Democrats of being so imbued with their own propaganda that they had effectively joined forces in blindly backing the euro.
The Communists (PCP), who also have 15 seats in parliament, say they oppose the euro because they do not want Portugal to lose control over its economic policy.
Economists said they doubted that any of Portugal's political parties would change their stance towards Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) over the next two years. PORTUGAL IN SOUND FINANCIAL POSITION
Portugal would not have to adopt austerity policies as harsh as those in some other European countries, they said.
It would not have to lay off civil servants or implement a public pay freeze.

Portugal also benefited from a privatisation programme that was expected to raised at least 460 billion escudos ($2.93 billion) this year -- two to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP). A similar sum is expected in 1997.

Economists said the state was unlikely to use its $5 billion in pure gold reserves as a cushion to meet EMU budget targets, although it could use gold to repay some state debt as long as it did not provoke a plunge in gold prices.
Portugal's biggest challenge in order to qualify for the euro was probably to bring down the budget deficit to the required three percent of GDP, they said.

Plans to cut the budget deficit to 2.9 percent of GDP in 1997 from 4.00 percent this year were based on optimistic economic growth projections that depended on factors outside Portugal's control, notably growth in Germany, Wilkinson said.
But the government has already made progress in bringing down inflation, the other main hurdle for EMU membership.
Consumer prices fell 0.1 percent in October, which enabled the government to cut three official interest rates in November.
Yield spreads over German government bonds have dropped to around 125 basis points from 520 in early 1995.
"Portugal's progress on inflation will depend a lot on the second half of 1997 when the economy is expected to start picking up," said Keith Edmonds, economist with IBJ.
Analysts said a final decision on joining the euro from the start in January 1999 would be a political one, rather than based on strict adhesion to economic guidelines.
"The key issue is not that Portugal's deficit is three percent of GDP, but Portugal's ability to show that keeping its deficit down is sustainable," said BPI's Martins dos Santos.

A Lisbon-based diplomat said: "The EU member states will not bend over backwards to let Portugal in. But if it becomes necessary to bend the criteria to let a major country in, then Portugal could crawl in under its coat tails."
D'Orey said a mood of euroscepticism could surface if Portugal's application to join EMU were rebuffed.

"If the EU were not flexible, there could be a backlash in Portugal in terms of anti-European feeling," he said. "The Portuguese would feel that those guys are cheating us as we made all the effort required of us." ($1=156.9 Escudo)
